introduction: Bahá’u’lláh begins with a man who sits among the shoes at the door while coveting the seat of honour: pride can dress as humility. The readings then follow it through its other clothes: learning, piety, office, dress, flattery, ancestry, the wish to lead, the servant who comes to think his station his own doing, and at the far end Pharaoh and Nimrod. The remedy offered is to look for one’s own faults and to remember where every gift came from. The Bible’s wisdom books and Gospels say much of this already, and they are joined here by Confucius, Lao Tzu, the Dhammapada, the Qur’án’s Iblís with his “I am better than him,” Shakespeare on brief authority, Gray, Shelley and Kipling on what becomes of glory, and Franklin, who admitted he would be proud of his humility. A different tradition deserves a hearing as well: Aristotle’s proper pride, Emerson’s self-trust, Whitman’s “divine am I,” and Browning’s reach that should exceed the grasp.
questions: The man by the door looks humble and is not. Jesus advises taking the lowest seat. How can a person tell humility from its imitation in himself?
“Man is noble,” and yet to think oneself superior is “a grievous error.” Where do Aristotle’s proper pride, Emerson’s self-trust and Whitman’s “divine am I” fall between those two statements?

The readings find pride among the learned and the clergy especially. Paul says knowledge puffs up; Pope says shallow learning intoxicates and deep learning sobers. What kind of learning produces humility?
Several readings describe a servant who came to believe that his honour was his own doing. What habits keep gratitude alive in someone who has been given a place of trust?
“One must not think of becoming a leader,” and Plato says the best-governed city is led by those most reluctant to rule. How, then, should responsibility be accepted when it comes?
Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar and Ozymandias all boast and fall. Kipling warned his own empire “lest we forget.” What does collective pride look like today, and who is in a position to name it?

outside.why: He “seateth himself amid the sandals by the door whilst coveting in his heart the seat of honour.” Jesus advises guests to take the lowest room, so that the host may say, Friend, go up higher. What separates his advice from the pose Bahá’u’lláh condemns?
Outward lowliness, inward appetite for honour. Jesus on the religious of his day: they love the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues, and to be called of men, Rabbi.
One “who wouldst appear as other than thou art.” Franklin caught the same thing in himself: had he overcome pride, he would probably be proud of his humility.

Another “layeth claim to inner knowledge, and still deeper knowledge.” Paul: knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth; if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know.
“Man is noble, for within all things the sign of God exists.” The eighth psalm: thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and hast crowned him with glory and honour.
To regard oneself as more learned or more God-fearing “is a grievous error.” Paul: in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
“Blessed is the learned one who prideth not himself on his knowledge.” Jeremiah: let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might.
The righteous one “revileth not the sinful.” Jesus to a crowd with stones in their hands: he that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.
“One must always search for his own shortcomings.” Lamentations: let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the Lord.
The search is the guard against pride. A disciple of Confucius: I daily examine myself on three points.
“The moment he considers himself good and says, ‘I am perfect’, he falls into pride and retrogresses.” Paul: let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.
One who regards himself as deficient progresses. The Dhammapada: the fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least so far; but a fool who thinks himself wise, he is called a fool indeed.
“They fall from their high pedestal and great is the noise thereof.” Proverbs: when pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom.
“Meekness and humility are the hallmarks of faith.” The shepherd boy’s song in The Pilgrim’s Progress: he that is down needs fear no fall, he that is low, no pride.
Whoever “prefers himself to his brother,” have no hope in him. In the Qur’án these are the first proud words ever spoken, by Iblís refusing to bow to Adam: I am better than him.
“One must never feel superior to anyone else.” Paul: not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly.
“Put away the garment of vainglory.” The First Letter of Peter names the garment to put on: be clothed with humility.
“Divest yourselves of the attire of haughtiness.” Luqmán to his son in the Qur’án: turn not thy cheek in scorn toward folk, nor walk with pertness in the land.
It does not befit one “created from dust” to swell with pride. Abraham, daring to plead with God: I, which am but dust and ashes.
Dust that will return to dust. The Qur’án: walk not in the earth exultant; thou canst not rend the earth, nor canst thou stretch to the height of the hills.
The globe is “a grain of poppy,” and man a part of it. Isaiah: the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance.
Vanity as “self-conceit and self-hypnotization.” The Preacher uses the word for everything under the sun: vanity of vanities; all is vanity.

One man works and says little; another “talks continually and boasts of his past achievements.” Confucius on the superior man: he acts before he speaks, and afterwards speaks according to his actions.
“Those who do most good say the least about it.” Jesus: when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth.
Good done quietly. The same sermon also says: let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works. How are the two sayings both kept?
Some will attack their friends’ motives “to gain a temporary applause.” Jesus: how can ye believe, which receive honour one of another, and seek not the honour that cometh from God only?
Their goal is that “people clap for them.” Jesus: take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them.
People who “live for dress.” The First Letter of Peter: whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, but the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit.
“They believe that God has created them for ‘Dress.’” Jesus: why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field.
Flattery and empty compliments “are no other than nets.” Proverbs has the same image: a man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet.
The crow believed the fox’s praise of its voice and lost what it held. Proverbs: let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips.
Some would give their lives “for the ephemeral fame of a few days.” Gray in the churchyard: the paths of glory lead but to the grave.
Name and fame: “no trace of them will remain.” Shelley’s traveller reads a king’s boast on a pedestal in the empty sands: look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair.
“One must not think of becoming a leader.” Plato: the State in which the rulers are most reluctant to govern is always the best and most quietly governed.
“Cast aside all mention of the ruler and the ruled.” Jesus: neither be ye called masters, for one is your Master; and all ye are brethren.
Whoever counts himself lowly “becomes glorified,” and whoever aspires to greatness falls. Jesus: whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.
A man strives day and night for the highest office. Macbeth, weighing what drives him: I have no spur but only vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself and falls on the other.
Nobles harbour “the melancholy of soaring ambition.” Milton gives the creed of it to Satan: better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven.

Desire for greatness is treated as a sickness of the great. Browning’s painter thinks a person without it has stopped living: a man’s reach should exceed his grasp, or what’s a heaven for? Which reaching do the readings condemn, and which would they bless?
Given a post and a salary, “he became so proud that he would not even speak with me.” Isabella in Measure for Measure: man, proud man, drest in a little brief authority.
A sudden promotion. The First Letter to Timothy on choosing leaders: not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall.
Those “enslaved by their lust for leadership.” The elder who wrote the Third Letter of John names one: Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them.

The “question of precedence” will come to matter after the first days. It came early among the disciples, at the last supper itself: there was also a strife among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest.
They are “fearful lest” they lose their place. John of the rulers who believed and kept quiet: they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.
They “follow the dictates of the leaders of their faith.” Jesus to those leaders: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered.
Proud talk of politics from people “completely unaware” of the subject. Proverbs: seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him.
A clergyman “may think that he knows more about God.” The Pharisee’s prayer: God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are.
“The humble man in his congregation may know more.” Jesus: thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes.
Knowledge was given for guidance, and its possessors grew proud against the Knower. Paul: the world by wisdom knew not God.
A divine “who carried volumes of books” did not recognize. The Qur’án’s image: the likeness of the ass carrying books.
The self-satisfied learned were deprived, and “you became privy to the mysteries.” Paul to Corinth: not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called.
A hundred years of study, and deprived “due to pride.” Socrates found himself wiser than the experts in one thing only: I neither know nor think that I know.
They “consider themselves the most exalted of creatures.” Paul: if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself.

Pride seizes a man for “the composition of two words.” Pope locates the danger in the amount: a little learning is a dangerous thing; shallow draughts intoxicate the brain, and drinking largely sobers us again. Is more learning a cure for the pride of learning?
Worshippers of “the idol which their imaginations have carved.” Xenophanes: if oxen and horses had hands, they would draw the forms of gods like their own.
One “maketh his asceticism his world.” Jesus on fasting for show: they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast.
A thousand prostrations a minute, “yet … steeped in pride.” Isaiah: this people draw near me with their mouth, but have removed their heart far from me.
The deed that makes for humility “is accepted by God.” Jesus of the publican who would not lift his eyes: this man went down to his house justified rather than the other.
Lowliness as strength. Lao Tzu: the rivers and seas receive the tribute of all the valley streams by their skill in being lower than they.
Pride “is the foundation of all vices.” Ben Sira said it two centuries before Christ: pride is the beginning of sin.

“Pride is the greatest sin - perhaps the only sin.” Isaiah’s taunt over a fallen king became the story of the first sin: thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven; I will be like the most High.

Pride is called perhaps the only sin. Aristotle counted a proper pride among the virtues and blamed its lack: the unduly humble man falls short both of his own merits and of the proud man’s claims. Is there a self-respect the readings would not call pride?

The proud are those who think themselves something. Whitman says it of himself with no apology: divine am I inside and out, and I make holy whatever I touch. Is this the pride the readings mean, or the nobility of the second reading?
Wealth “makes a person self-centered … forgetful of God.” Moses: and thou say in thine heart, My power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth.
Wealth draws its victims on. The Qur’án on Korah, whose treasure-keys were a burden for strong men: his people said unto him, Exult not; Allah loveth not the exultant.

People in the mud who say, “we are suns and stars; we are not in need of thy education.” The letter to Laodicea: thou sayest, I am rich, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and poor, and blind.
“They are blind but suppose themselves” all-seeing. Jesus: if ye were blind, ye should have no sin: but now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá would not write while his Father’s pen was heard. John the Baptist: he must increase, but I must decrease.
Some “attributed this blessing and bounty to their own wisdom and efforts.” Paul: what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory?
The honour was grace. A psalm: not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory.
They “imagined that they had some merit … of their own.” John the Baptist: a man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven.
They “did not appreciate the value of these bounties.” Moses: when thou hast eaten and art full, beware that thou forget not the Lord thy God.
One whose cause was exalted, who “waxed proud before Him Who created” him. Samuel to Saul: when thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel?
“We chose one of our brothers and elevated him to a station where pride … seized him.” The Chronicler of King Uzziah: when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction.
“I have labored more for You … and You do not appreciate my labors.” The elder brother in the parable: lo, these many years do I serve thee, and yet thou never gavest me a kid.
A secretary came to think his station “was of his own doing.” Miriam and Aaron of Moses: hath the Lord indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us?
“In any cycle or time someone has shown pride.” Korah to Moses and Aaron: ye take too much upon you, seeing all the congregation are holy; wherefore then lift ye up yourselves?
“We are the descendants of Rustam the mighty!” John the Baptist: think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father; God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.
A prime minister has an ancestry found for him. The rhyme of the English rising of 1381: when Adam delved and Eve span, who was then a gentleman?
A pedigree celebrated. Burns: the rank is but the guinea’s stamp, the man’s the gold for all that.
“Observe what things men vaunt themselves over!” Paul lists his own pedigree, a Hebrew of the Hebrews, and then: what things were gain to me, those I counted loss.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes Pharaoh’s boast. Here is the verse: O my people! Is not mine the sovereignty of Egypt and these rivers flowing under me?

Great cities and conquering armies, gone in a brief time. Nebuchadnezzar on his palace roof: is not this great Babylon, that I have built by the might of my power? While the word was in his mouth, the kingdom departed from him.
“Each became a mighty Pharaoh.” The original: who is the Lord, that I should obey his voice?
A sultan “exhibited pride.” Kipling’s hymn for an empire at its height, in 1897: lo, all our pomp of yesterday is one with Nineveh and Tyre.
“Be not proud before Him.” James, quoting Proverbs: God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.
All necks bowed, “while the proud were in the fire.” Mary’s song: he hath scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts; he hath put down the mighty from their seats.
The guide quotes Proverbs on pride before a fall. Obadiah to a mountain kingdom: the pride of thine heart hath deceived thee; though thou exalt thyself as the eagle, thence will I bring thee down.

Dignity and respect for others belong to a community’s health; pride does not. Confucius draws the same line: the superior man has a dignified ease without pride; the mean man has pride without a dignified ease.

Self-aggrandisement is “among the most deadly of sins.” Emerson built an ethic on confidence in oneself: trust thyself; every heart vibrates to that iron string. Where does self-trust end and self-aggrandisement begin?
Believers must recognize “intellectual honesty and humility” and not define what is beyond them. Paul: we know in part, and we prophesy in part.

daniel-is-not-this-great-babylon.text: The king spake, and said, Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty

timothy-lifted-up-with-pride.text: Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil

samuel-little-in-thine-own-sight.text: And Samuel said, When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel, and the Lord anointed thee king over Israel

chronicles-heart-was-lifted-up.text: But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the Lord his God, and went into the temple of the Lord to burn incense upon the altar of incense

numbers-hath-he-not-spoken-also-by-us.text: And Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married: for he had married an Ethiopian woman. And they said, Hath the Lord indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us? And the Lord heard it

john-epistle-loveth-to-have-the-preemine.text: I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not

luke-which-should-be-accounted-the-great.text: And there was also a strife among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest

obadiah-pride-of-thine-heart.text: The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee, thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, whose habitation is high; that saith in his heart, Who shall bring me down to the ground? Though thou exalt thyself as the eagle, and though thou set thy nest among the stars, thence will I bring thee down, saith the Lord

proverbs-pride-shall-bring-him-low.text: A man's pride shall bring him low: but honour shall uphold the humble in spirit

proverbs-when-pride-cometh.text: When pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom

quran-is-not-mine-the-sovereignty-of-egy.text: And Pharaoh caused a proclamation to be made among his people saying: O my people! Is not mine the sovereignty of Egypt and these rivers flowing under me? Can ye not then discern?

quran-i-am-better-than-him.text: He said: What hindered thee that thou didst not fall prostrate when I bade thee? (Iblis) said: I am better than him. Thou createdst me of fire while him Thou didst create of mud.

sirach-pride-is-the-beginning-of-sin.text: For pride is the beginning of sin, and he that hath it shall pour out abomination
